detailHeading: Why woodwork moves in Georgian Bay homes
detailBody: Wood swells in humid summers and shrinks when the furnace runs all winter. Around Collingwood and Nottawasaga Bay, the swing is wide. Doors start to stick, mitred trim joints open, and caulk lines crack at the corners.

Exterior wood takes the most abuse. Window sills, door thresholds and deck boards sit wet through spring melt and freeze-thaw cycles. Soft spots, peeling paint and dark stains are early signs of rot. Catching rot early keeps the repair small, often a sill or a few boards instead of the framing below.

Older homes and cottages bring their own quirks. Walls are rarely square and floors are rarely level. Keith scribes and shims trim to fit what is there and matches existing profiles where possible, so a repair blends with the rest of the room.

faqs.q: Will new trim match my existing woodwork?
faqs.a: Keith looks at the profile, size and wood species and sources the closest match. Older or custom profiles are harder to find, so he talks through options, such as replacing the trim on a full wall for a consistent look.

faqs.q: Do you paint or stain the finished work?
faqs.a: Yes. Keith fills nail holes, sands and prepares new woodwork for paint or stain. He applies the finish too if you want one person to handle the whole job from start to finish.

faqs.q: How do you handle rot repair?
faqs.a: Keith removes the soft wood until he reaches solid material, then replaces the damaged section. He also looks for the source of the water, such as missing flashing or a failed caulk joint, so the rot does not return.

faqs.q: What about damaged framing or subfloor?
faqs.a: Keith looks at damaged joists, framing and subfloor during the estimate. Larger structural work is scoped with care, and any specialist requirement is identified in the estimate before work begins.

faqs.q: Do you take on small carpentry jobs?
faqs.a: Yes. A single sticking door, a cracked casing or one loose stair railing is worth a call. Keith also groups small items into one visit so your whole list gets done together.

detailBody: Caulk is the first line of defence at every tub and shower joint. Watch for black spots under the surface, edges lifting away from the tile, gaps at the corners and soft grout nearby. Mould under the bead usually means water has already worked behind the seal.

Fresh caulk over old caulk rarely lasts. The new bead bonds to the failing one, not to the tile or tub. Keith removes the old material completely, cleans and dries the joint, then applies a mould-resistant silicone in one continuous bead.

Cottage bathrooms see extra stress. A cold, closed building over winter and a humid, busy summer make joints expand and shrink. A spring check of the caulk lines before the first guests arrive catches small gaps early.

faqs.q: How do I know when caulk needs replacing?
faqs.a: Look for cracks, peeling edges, gaps at the corners or mould you cannot wipe away. If water sits in the joint or the bead feels soft, the seal has failed. Replacing failing caulk early protects the subfloor and wall framing.

faqs.q: Why not caulk over the old bead?
faqs.a: New caulk does not bond well to old caulk, soap film or mould. The fresh bead peels away and traps moisture behind the seal. Full removal and a clean, dry surface give the new caulk a proper bond.

faqs.q: When is the shower ready to use again?
faqs.a: Silicone needs time to cure before water touches the joint. Keith follows the cure time on the product label and tells you when the shower is ready. Plan for the tub or shower to stay out of use until then.

faqs.q: What if you find water damage behind the caulk?
faqs.a: Keith shows you what he finds and explains the options before going further. Soft drywall, loose tile or rotted subfloor is added to the estimate, and any work needing a licensed plumber is coordinated with a licensed trade.

faqs.q: Do I need to do anything to prepare?
faqs.a: Clear bottles, mats and shower caddies from the area. Avoid running the tub or shower right before the visit so the joints start dry. Keith handles the rest, including the cleanup.

detailHeading: What makes tile last in a Collingwood home
detailBody: Most tile failures start below the tile. A floor with too much bounce cracks grout lines. A shower wall without a waterproof membrane lets water into the framing. Keith checks the subfloor and walls first and adds backer board, membrane or levelling where the job needs them.

Entryways and mudrooms take hard wear in this area. Beach sand in summer and road salt and slush in winter grind at grout. A durable floor tile, a sealed or stain-resistant grout and a good mat at the door all help.
Layout matters as much as materials. Keith plans the reference lines so cuts land at the edges of the room, not in the middle of the floor, and so the pattern lines up with doors and counters.

faqs.q: Will you install tile I already bought?
faqs.a: Yes. Keith installs tile you supply. Before work starts, check the boxes share the same lot number and order extra for cuts and future repairs. Keith confirms the setting materials and trim pieces the job needs.

faqs.q: Do I need backer board or a membrane?
faqs.a: Wet areas such as shower walls and tub surrounds need a waterproof membrane or a waterproof backer system. Floors need a flat, stiff base. Keith looks at the existing surface during the estimate and explains what your space needs.

faqs.q: Is matching existing tile possible for a repair?
faqs.a: Often, if you kept spare tiles from the original job. If not, Keith helps you look for a close match. For a consistent look, some homeowners replace a full area, such as a backsplash wall, instead of a few tiles.

faqs.q: How do I care for new tile?
faqs.a: Wipe up spills and clean with a pH-neutral cleaner. Reseal cement grout on the schedule the grout maker recommends, especially in showers. Keep a mat at entry doors to catch sand and salt before they reach the tile.

faqs.q: Do you tile cottage bathrooms and entryways?

detailHeading: Choosing the height and wall for your TV
detailBody: The most common mistake is mounting a TV too high. For seated viewing, the centre of the screen sits best close to eye level from the couch. Above a fireplace, a tilting or pull-down mount brings the picture back toward a comfortable angle.

The wall matters as much as the mount. Drywall needs studs or added blocking. Plaster walls in older homes crack without careful drilling. Brick, stone and log walls in cottages need anchors suited to masonry or solid wood. Keith checks the wall before choosing hardware.

Plan the cables before the mount goes up. Low-voltage HDMI and network cables run inside the wall with the right kit. A new power outlet behind the TV is electrical work, so where the job needs a licensed electrician, the work is arranged with one.

faqs.q: What size TVs do you mount?
faqs.a: Keith mounts most flat-screen sizes, from a small bedroom TV to a large living room screen. The limit comes from the mount rating and the wall. He checks both and uses hardware rated above the weight of your TV.

faqs.q: Do I need to supply the mount?
faqs.a: Either way works. Buy a mount rated for your TV’s size and weight, or ask Keith to recommend a fixed, tilting or full-motion style for the room. Have the TV’s model number ready so the mount pattern matches.

faqs.q: Will the cables be hidden?
faqs.a: Cords are hidden with a paintable raceway on the wall or routed inside the wall with a low-voltage kit. Where the job needs a new outlet behind the TV, a licensed electrician handles the electrical part.

faqs.q: Do you mount on brick, stone or plaster?
faqs.a: Yes. Each wall type needs different anchors and drilling. Keith checks the wall during the estimate, chooses fasteners suited to the material and protects the surface while drilling.

faqs.q: Do you mount TVs outdoors?
faqs.a: Yes, on covered porches and patios. Outdoor setups need a weather-rated mount and a TV made for outdoor use or kept under good cover. Any new exterior outlet is arranged with a licensed electrician.

detailHeading: Paint choices for Georgian Bay weather
detailBody: Preparation decides how long paint lasts. Keith fills holes, sands rough patches, cleans greasy or dusty surfaces and spot-primes repairs before the finish coats. Skipping this step shows up as peeling, uneven sheen or patches visible through the new colour.

Bathrooms and cottage kitchens see heavy humidity. A mould-resistant paint in a satin or semi-gloss sheen holds up better than flat paint in these rooms, and a working exhaust fan matters as much as the paint. Keith suggests products for each room during the estimate.

Exterior painting depends on the weather. Paint needs dry surfaces and temperatures within the range on the label, so most exterior work around Collingwood happens from late spring to early fall. Walls facing south and west take the most sun and fade first.

faqs.q: Do I need to move my furniture?
faqs.a: Move small items, art and breakables before the visit. Keith moves larger furniture to the centre of the room, covers everything and protects the floors. Mention anything fragile or heavy during the estimate.

faqs.q: When is the best time for exterior painting?
faqs.a: Late spring to early fall brings the dry days and temperatures exterior paint needs. Surfaces must be dry, and cool, damp nights near the water slow drying. Book the estimate early in the year to plan around the weather.

faqs.q: Will touch-ups match my existing colour?
faqs.a: Keep leftover paint or the colour name if you have them. A paint store matches a colour from a small chip too. Touch-ups on older paint sometimes show, so Keith often suggests repainting a full wall for an even look.

faqs.q: Do you paint kitchen cabinets?
faqs.a: Yes. Cabinet painting needs careful cleaning, sanding and a hard-wearing finish. See the kitchen cabinet painting page for how Keith handles doors, boxes and hardware.

Turnovers are the best time to catch up. With the unit empty, Keith patches and paints walls, fixes doors and trim, re-caulks tubs and sinks, and checks smoke and carbon monoxide alarms before the next tenant moves in. Photos of finished items go into your records.

Rental cottages and seasonal units around Georgian Bay add more work. Opening and closing, storm checks and freeze protection fit into the same maintenance plan. Work needing a licensed plumber, electrician or gas technician is identified and coordinated with a licensed trade.

seoDescription: Cottage closing around Collingwood and Georgian Bay by Keith Diver. Water drained, gaps sealed, cottage secured. Call 705-795-4009 for a free estimate.
h1: Cottage closing to protect your property over winter.
sub: Keith drains water lines, seals entry points and secures your cottage for winter, with well and gas shutdowns coordinated with licensed trades.
cardsIntro: Keith handles cottage closing in Collingwood, Wasaga Beach and Oro-Medonte, so your property is ready for freezing weather before you head home.

cards.title: Water drain-down
cards.body: Shut off the supply, open taps and drain lines, and add plumbing antifreeze to traps and toilets to protect against freezing.

cards.title: Well & gas shutdown
cards.body: Well pump, pressure tank, water heater and gas appliance shutdowns are coordinated with a licensed plumber or gas technician.

cards.title: Pest prevention
cards.body: Seal small gaps, remove food, prop open the fridge and close up the spots mice use to get inside over winter.

cards.title: Secure & document
cards.body: Store outdoor furniture, check every door and window lock, and photograph the cottage so you have a record of its condition.

scopeNote: Project scope and any specialist trade requirements are confirmed before work begins.
processHeading: From last weekend to locked up for winter.

steps.title: Tell me about your cottage
steps.body: Share the location, the water and heat systems, and when you plan to leave for the season.

steps.title: Review your estimate
steps.body: Go over a clear estimate for the closing tasks and any trade work for the well or gas appliances.

steps.title: Plan the work
steps.body: Confirm access details and whether you want winter checks before work begins.

detailHeading: Why a careful closing matters on Georgian Bay
detailBody: Water left in a pipe, trap or fixture expands when frozen and cracks the fitting. The leak stays hidden until spring, when the water goes back on. A careful drain-down and plumbing antifreeze in every trap and toilet protect the system through the coldest months.

Closing also means keeping animals and weather out. Mice look for warm, quiet buildings in the fall. Keith seals small gaps, removes food and other attractants, and stores outdoor furniture and cushions before snow arrives.

Owners who are away share access details and a contact for decisions. Shutdown of a well pump, pressure tank, water heater or gas appliance is coordinated with a licensed plumber or gas technician. Ask about winter checks if your insurer requires visits to a vacant cottage.

faqs.q: When should I close my cottage?
faqs.a: Close before the first hard frost, once you are done with the season. Waiting too long risks a cold snap before the lines are drained. Book early in the fall, since many owners close around the same weekends.

faqs.q: Do you drain the water heater?
faqs.a: The water heater is part of the closing plan. Draining or shutting down a gas water heater, along with any other gas appliance, is coordinated with a licensed gas technician. Keith confirms who handles each step in the estimate.

faqs.q: What happens if the lines are not drained properly?
faqs.a: Water left in a line or fitting freezes, expands and cracks the pipe. The damage often stays hidden until spring, when the water goes back on and the leak soaks floors, walls or cabinets.

faqs.q: Should I leave some heat on?
faqs.a: Some owners keep low heat on all winter, others shut the heat off and fully drain the system. The right choice depends on the building and your insurance. Keith talks through both, and furnace or gas work goes to a licensed technician.

faqs.q: Do you offer winter checks after closing?
faqs.a: Yes. Keith offers property checks through the off-season, with photos after each visit. See the cottage maintenance page for what a check covers, or ask about combining closing, winter checks and spring opening.

h1: Tenant placement prep for a unit ready to rent.
sub: Keith handles the repairs, safety checks and photos landlords need between tenants, so the unit is ready to show and ready for move-in.
cardsHeading: Get the unit ready for the next tenant.
cardsIntro: Keith prepares rental units for tenant placement in Collingwood, Wasaga Beach and Stayner, as part of property care for landlords and property managers.

cards.title: Pre-listing walk-through
cards.body: Walk the unit with you, or on your behalf, and build a punch list of repairs, touch-ups and safety items.

cards.title: Turnover repairs
cards.body: Patch drywall, touch up paint, fix trim and flooring damage, and re-caulk tubs and counters before the unit is listed.

cards.title: Locks & alarms
cards.body: Re-key or replace locks between tenants, and test smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, replacing battery units where needed.

cards.title: Photos & access
cards.body: Before-and-after photos for your listing and move-in records, and help coordinating access for showings with you or your leasing agent.

steps.body: Share the address, the move-out date and any repairs or concerns you have noted.

steps.title: Review your estimate
steps.body: Go over a clear estimate for the punch list, including scope and any trade requirements.

steps.title: Plan the work
steps.body: Confirm access, the punch list and the next steps before work begins.

detailHeading: What Keith handles, and what stays with the landlord
detailBody: Tenant placement has two sides. One is the physical unit: repairs, paint, locks, alarms and a clean, documented handover. The other is finding and signing the tenant. Keith handles the first part, as part of property care for landlords and property managers.

Keith does not screen tenants, prepare leases or give legal advice. Landlords should follow the Ontario Residential Tenancies Act and use the Ontario standard lease form. Questions about screening, rent or tenant rights belong with a lawyer, a paralegal or the Landlord and Tenant Board.

A well-prepared unit helps on both sides. Clear photos support your listing, and a documented move-in condition gives you and the tenant a shared record. Work needing a licensed plumber or electrician is identified in the estimate and coordinated with a licensed trade.

faqs.q: Do you screen tenants or sign leases?
faqs.a: No. Keith prepares the unit, and the landlord or property manager handles screening, the lease and the tenancy. Follow the Ontario Residential Tenancies Act and use the Ontario standard lease form. For legal questions, speak with a lawyer or paralegal.

faqs.q: Do you coordinate access for showings?
faqs.a: Yes. Keith coordinates access with you or your leasing agent, such as a lockbox arrangement, so the unit is available for showings while the turnover work is under way or once the work is done.

faqs.q: Do you work with property managers on several units?
faqs.a: Yes. Keith works with self-managing landlords and property managers on single units and on several properties. Share your locations and the turnover work you send out most so visits are planned well.

faqs.q: Do the photos help with my move-in records?
faqs.a: Yes. Keith takes before-and-after photos of completed items. Use them in your listing and keep them with your move-in condition record, alongside the walk-through you do with the new tenant.

faqs.q: Which areas do you cover?
faqs.a: Keith is based in Collingwood and prepares rental units in Wasaga Beach, Stayner, Barrie and nearby communities. Include the address when you ask for an estimate.
